paras: The Grant Parish seed-store shooting was a night attack in mid-September 1880 in which a party of unknown men fired into a cotton-seed store kept by Israel Smith, a Black man, about five miles south of Colfax, Louisiana, killing a boy of about 18 who was sleeping inside. The same party then fired into a second seed store owned by white men, wounding no one. The local Colfax Chronicle condemned the killing, and in December it linked the attackers to the burning of the same store.

On a Wednesday night, probably September 15, the attackers fired without warning into Smith's store, where Smith, another man and the boy were sleeping. The boy was killed instantly and the two men escaped unhurt. From there the party went to a seed store belonging to L. E. Torry and S. M. Lacroix of Colfax and "riddled it with bullets" while W. B. Hopkins slept inside; he was not hurt, and the paper noted that all connected with that store were white men. The victim was not named; in December the Chronicle described him as a young Black man killed by shots fired through the store's walls.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. On a Thursday night in early December the store, by then owned by Smith and Hansom Brisco, was burned while volleys were fired into it, and the Chronicle wrote that the arsonists were "evidently the same set" who had killed the young man there in the fall. Smith told the paper he had no clue whether the party was made up of white or Black men.

The Colfax Chronicle ran the first report under the headline "The Bloody Regulators," calling the killing "midnight assassination" and demanding that those responsible be "hunted down by the strong arm of the law." Its condemnation was qualified: it called the cotton-seed business "most nefarious" and repeated the opinion that the attackers had not meant to take life, while insisting that this was no excuse. In December, under "Murderous Incendiaries," the paper called the attackers "cut-throats" and declared that "These negroes are entitled to protection."

Outside Grant Parish the story traveled only through state-news roundups: the St. Landry Democrat reprinted the September news paragraphs on October 9 without the editorial, and the Donaldsonville Chief reprinted the December item on December 25.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle local report (September)
accounts.gist: Unknown men fired into Smith's seed store, killing a boy of about 18, then fired into a white-owned seed store without hurting its occupant.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle retrospective (December)
accounts.gist: Reporting the burning of the same store, the paper said the arsonists were evidently the set who had killed a young Black man there in the fall by shooting through the walls.

framing.detail: Headlined 'The Bloody Regulators'; called the killing 'midnight assassination' and 'attrocious barbarism' while calling the cotton-seed business 'most nefarious'.
In December, under 'Murderous Incendiaries', called the attackers 'cut-throats' and said 'These negroes are entitled to protection'.
The St. Landry Democrat and Donaldsonville Chief reprinted the Chronicle's news paragraphs in state-news roundups without comment.
